Urban Analytics and City Science Assessment 2051924

2024-12-01

Introduction

Social networks exist on a diverse scale, ranging from the interactions between individual people and places to communities, aggregated localities and countries. These social interactions take place in many forms and propagate across multiple dimensions (Bardis, 1979). One example that embodies such characteristics is Social Media; simultaneously abstract and digital but also a reflection of real world phenomena and lived social interactions. The analysis of social media networks therefore provides an opportunity to explore real social networks using readily available data. One such example is the Facebook Social Connectedness Index.

The Facebook Social Connectedness Index (SCI) is an aggregated, depersonalised metric that captures the general probability of a facebook friendship connection between nations or geographic subdivisions, derived from facebook user data. As Bailey et al., 2018 (see p. 261) argues, since facebook friendships are primarily grounded in real-world connections, this dataset provides a valuable insight into global connectivity across multiple scales. The dataset has been used widely, both as a predictor of other factors such as international trade (Bailey et al., 2020b), pandemic dispersion (Prusaczyk et al., 2021), and to determine predictors of SCI itself. It is the latter goal that forms the core of this study. There exists many such studies, examining a wide range of the socio-economic and political determinants of SCI (See Bailey et al., 2020a, Bailey et al., 2018, Gavriilidis, 2020). However, there is a noted lack of cultural and semantic explanations of SCI in the literature; despite a strong corpus of research to confirm their importance in human connection (See Geertz., 1973 for a concise overview)

One such example, Bailey et al., 2020c, examines language and religious similarity alongside other variables in predicting European SCI, but does not consider global connectedness. The aim of this paper therefore is to build upon this past research by investigating the validity and usefulness of language and religion to predict the connectivity of the global network of nations.

Methodology

Data - analysis and transformations

As mentioned, the primary dataset used in this report is the Facebook Social Connectedness Index, provided on an open license basis by META (See Bailey et al., 2018). The data is provided in many forms of geographic scale; the broadest of these was chosen for this research project. Specifically, country pairings of SCI, as determined by the following equation:

\[ SCI_{i,j} = \frac{\text{Facebook Connections}_{i,j}}{\text{Facebook Users}_i \times \text{Facebook Users}_j} \]

Country pairings were chosen over more resolute datasets, including administrative subdivisions and US counties, to broaden the scope of the project and improve computational efficiency. Figure 1 below demonstrates the global network of country connections.

# Downloading world map from GiTHUB
devtools::install_github("ropensci/rnaturalearthhires")

# Use ne_countries function to obtain world shapefile
world <- ne_countries(scale = "large", type = "countries", returnclass = "sf")

# Selecting only the two letter country code and geometry columns
world_trim <- world %>%
  select(iso_a2, geometry)

# Making geometries valid
world_trim_valid <- st_make_valid(world_trim)

# Calculating centroids of each country polygon
world_centroids <- st_centroid(world_trim_valid) 

# Preparing the graph for plotting - create country coordinate data frame
country_coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(world_centroids))

countries_in_network <- unique(c(fb_cnt_sci$user_loc, fb_cnt_sci$fr_loc))

# Filter the country_coords data to include only the countries present in the network
filtered_country_coords <- country_coords[country_coords$country %in% countries_in_network, ]

# Attempting to data wrangle missing country data - using setdiff() to identify missing coordinates
missing_in_coords <- setdiff(countries_in_network, filtered_country_coords$country)

# Manually add coordinates for missing countries
missing_coords <- data.frame(
  country = c("FR", "GF", "GP", "MQ", "RE", "YT", "TW", "XK", "NO"),

)

# Creating spatial object out of country coordinate dataframe
centroids_sf <- st_as_sf(filtered_country_coords, coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = 4326)

# Merging SCI data with centroids dataframe
connections_sf <- fb_cnt_sci %>%
  left_join(filtered_country_coords, by = c("user_loc" = "country")) %>%
  rename(lon1 = X, lat1 = Y) %>%

connections_sf$scaled_sci_log <- log(connections_sf$scaled_sci + 1)


# Plot the world basemap

  geom_sf(data = centroids_sf, color = "grey", size = 2) +  # Centroids (dots)

Figure 1: World Map of logged Facebook Social Connectedness Index for country pairs. Linewidth indicates connectedness, grey points denote country centroids

To complement the data above, 3 other data sets were used in this analysis. To investigate the impacts of linguistic similarity on SCI, the ‘language’ data set provided by the Centre d’Etudes Prospectives et d’Informations Internationales (CEPII) was accessed under an open licence (See Melitz and Toubal, 2014). This data set includes a variety of aggregated metrics to estimate the language similarity between nations, the full extent of which may be seen at Melitz and Toubal, 2014. For this project, the common language index was extracted. To estimate the similarity of religious composition between nations, the ‘The Future of World Religions: Population Growth Projections, 2010-2050’ data, provided by the Pew Research Center, was imported (Pew Reserach Center, 2015). Data was filtered for 2020, to be most respective of the temporal scale of the SCI data, and then a similarity metric was calculated using the inverse of euclidean distance, as seen below. 

# Creating aggregated similarity metric for religion

r_countries <- religion_data$Country # Extracting country names 
religion_data <- religion_data[,-1] # Removing name column
rownames(religion_data) <- r_countries # Setting country names as row names

# Data frame is ready, but was read in as character file so setting to be numeric
# Function below: removes < or > symbols for numeric conversion 
religion_data[] <- lapply(religion_data, function(x) {
  # Replace occurrences of '> 99.0' with '99.5'
  x <- gsub(">99.0", "99.5", x)  
  
  # Replace '< 1.0' values with '0.1'
  x <- gsub("< 1.0", "0.1", x)  
  # Convert to numeric
  as.numeric(x)
})


# Calculate euclidean distance
dist_matrix <- dist(religion_data, method = "euclidean")

# Convert to similarity (1 / (1 + Euclidean distance))

similarity_matrix <- 1 / (1 + dist_matrix)

# Convert to matrix
similarity_matrix <- as.matrix(similarity_matrix)

Euclidean distance was also used to calculate the similarity of GDP per capita between country pairs, following scaling to a median of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Scaling was performed to normalise the large variation present. The data was provided on an open source license by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) through the World Economic Outlook for October 2021 (IMF, 2021). This temporal scale was chosen to roughly match those of religious similarity and the SCI data. GDP per capita was chosen for inclusion to act as a generalised proxy for the socio-economic characteristics of nations, informed by previous studies, such as Bailey et al., 2020b, that have found it an important control on SCI. This aggregated similarity metric was produced using the following code

# Creating a euclidean distance based 'similarity metric' for gdp per capita as a control of socio-economic similarity

gdp_pc$gdp_pc <- as.numeric(gdp_pc$gdp_pc) # set to numeric

gdp_pc_clean <- gdp_pc %>% filter(!grepl("no data", gdp_pc, ignore.case = TRUE)) # remove 'no data' values

rownames(gdp_pc_clean) <- gdp_pc_clean$country # set rownames of dataset to country names

gdp_pc_clean <- select(gdp_pc_clean, "gdp_pc") # remove country column and retain gdp data
gdp_pc_clean$gdp_pc <- as.numeric(gdp_pc_clean$gdp_pc)

# scaling the data
gdp_scaled <- scale(gdp_pc_clean)

# Creating distance matrix
gdp_dist <- dist(gdp_pc_clean, method = "euclidean") 

# Calculate similarity: 1 / (1 + distance)
gdp_similarity <- 1 / (1 + gdp_dist)
gdp_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(gdp_similarity)

Geographic distance is a proven control on country-country SCI (Bailey et al., 2018), and so was included in the analysis of this report to act as a control variable while investigating the impacts of language and religion on inter-country SCI. To create a geographic distance dataset, a shapefile of the world was downloaded using the rnaturalearth package (Massicote and South, 2024) and then the centroids of each country polygon inferred using the st_centroids function from the SF package (Pebesma, E. 2018). Following the manual interpolation of country centroids included in the SCI dataset, but missing in the world shapefile, an iterative loop was created to fill an empty matrix with country coordinates and then distances calculated using the distVincentysphere function from the geosphere package (Hijmans. RJ, 2018) to calculate the distances between. The resulting matrix was then transformed into a dataframe for use with other data.

# Making geometries valid

world_trim_valid <- st_make_valid(world_trim)

# Calculating centroids of each country polygon
world_centroids <- st_centroid(world_trim_valid) 


# Preparing the graph for plotting

country_coords$country <- world_centroids$iso_a2

# Standardizing names so that only centroids from countries in the SCI dataset are included (this also avoids errors in inputting countrys as vertices)
# Combine both columns into a single vector of country names

countries_in_network <- unique(c(fb_cnt_cnt$user_loc, fb_cnt_cnt$fr_loc))

# Filter the country_coords data to include only the countries present in the network
filtered_country_coords <- country_coords[country_coords$country %in% countries_in_network, ]

# attempting to data wrangle country data and deduce missing centroids

missing_in_coords <- setdiff(countries_in_network, filtered_country_coords$country)



# Manually add coordinates for missing centroids
missing_coords <- data.frame(
  country = c("FR", "GF", "GP", "MQ", "RE", "YT", "TW", "XK", "NO"),
  X = c(2.2137, -53.125, -61.527, -61.024, 55.236, 45.228, 121.5654, 20.911, 10.7522),
  Y = c(46.6034, 3.9332, 16.265, 14.641, -21.115, -12.836, 23.6978, 42.6025, 59.9139)
)


# Add missing country coordinates to the filtered dataset
filtered_country_coords <- rbind(filtered_country_coords, missing_coords)

# Create a matrix to store distances
n <- nrow(spatial_df)
distance_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = n, ncol = n)

# Loop over all pairs of countries to calculate distances
for (i in 1:n) {
  for (j in 1:n) {
    # Get coordinates for country i and country j
    point_i <- c(spatial_df$X[i], spatial_df$Y[i])  # point_i as a vector (longitude, latitude)
    point_j <- c(spatial_df$X[j], spatial_df$Y[j])  # point_j as a vector (longitude, latitude)
    
    # Check if the points are being formed correctly
    print(paste("point_i:", point_i))
    print(paste("point_j:", point_j))
    
    # Calculate the distance using distVincentySphere
    distance_matrix[i, j] <- distVincentySphere(point_i, point_j)
  }
}

# Convert the distance matrix into a 3-column dataframe with country-country pairs and distances
distance_df <- data.frame(
  country1 = rep(spatial_df$country, each = n),
  country2 = rep(spatial_df$country, times = n),
  distance = as.vector(distance_matrix)
)

# Remove duplicate rows and then view for validity
distance_df <- distance_df[distance_df$country1 < distance_df$country2, ]

head(distance_df) 

# Distance dataframe uses ISO2 so add country names using the country code package for ease of binding

distance_df$country1_name <- countrycode(distance_df$country1, "iso2c", "country.name")
distance_df$country2_name <- countrycode(distance_df$country2, "iso2c", "country.name")

Network Analysis and Community Detection

Network analysis methods were employed on the SCI dataset to investigate the characteristics and nature of the country relations. The SCI dataset is weighted and undirectional, therefore the following metrics were analyzed: Weighted Degree, Betweeness Centrality, Closeness Centrality and Eigenvector centrality. All of these were created using the igraph package (Csárdi et al., 2024), and then tabulated using the stargazer package (Hlavac M., 2022). For representation in this report, 20 countries were chosen based on their strategic importance in global affairs, and their contextual relationship with Religious and Linguistic international dynamics (See Fox., 2008 and Grimes., 1986). A full table of all country network metrics is included in the Appendix.

# Create igraph object from SCI data
g <- graph_from_data_frame(fb_cnt_sci, directed = FALSE)
E(g)$weight <- fb_cnt_sci$scaled_sci # activate edges and weight as sci
# Degree (weighted)
degree_weighted <- strength(g, mode = "all")

# Betweenness Centrality
betweenness_centrality <- betweenness(g, directed = FALSE)

# Closeness Centrality
closeness_centrality <- closeness(g, mode = "all")

# Eigenvector Centrality
eigenvector_centrality <- eigen_centrality(g)$vector



# Combine metrics into a data frame
metrics_df <- data.frame(
  Country = V(g)$name,
  Weighted_Degree = degree_weighted,
  Betweenness = betweenness_centrality,
  Closeness = closeness_centrality,
  Eigenvector = eigenvector_centrality,
)

# Write to file - code was precomputed using the above methodology and read in at the start of the document
#write.csv(metrics_df, "metrics_df.csv")


# Selecting subset of 20 countries:
# list of selected ISO2 country codes
selected_countries <- c("US", "AU", "IN", "GB", "BR", "CA", "DE", "ID", 
                        "MX", "FR", "PK", "NG", "TR", "JP", "ZA", "EG", 
                        "IT", "SA", "AR", "KR")

# Subset the dataset based on the country column (ISO2 code)
subset_df <- metrics_df[metrics_df$Country %in% selected_countries, ]

#add country names to the dataset and remove ISO2 codes
subset_df$Country <- countrycode(subset_df$Country, origin = "iso2c", destination = "country.name")

# Metrics calculated and saved to file, then imported for computational efficiency using following code

#write.csv(subset_df, "subset_metrics_df.csv")

To highlight the network characteristics of the data, a Louvain community detection algorithim was used to identify community groups within the data (See Blondel et al., 2008). This was method chosen due to its strength in detecting modular structures and capacity for working with weighted networks. Community detection and respective modularity score was calculated using the ‘cluster_louvain’ and ‘modularity’ functions from the igraph package.

# Modularity (using Louvain method for community detection)
community_louvain <- cluster_louvain(g)
modularity_score <- modularity(community_louvain)

Regression Models

To investigate the specific controls on SCI when determined by linguistic and religious similarity, multiple regression models were created. The regression models measured logged SCI as an independent variable in the equation as follows. SCI was logged to minimize variance in the data.

\[ \log(\text{scaled_SCI}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{religious_similarity} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{cle} + \beta_3 \cdot \text{distance} + \beta_4 \cdot \text{GDP_pc_Similarity} + \epsilon \]

Due to methodological differences in the data, incomplete and missing values were present in all fields (excluding SCI). Therefore two aggregated datasets were used for regression analysis. One which excluded all country-country rows with missing values, and another that used K Nearest Neighbours (kNN) imputation. A random seed was set for reproducibility, and k was set as 5 to balance simplicity and validity. Interpolation was performed using the kNN function from the VIM package (Kowarik and Templ, 2016). Following this, 3 regression models were created. Two linear regression models using the aforely mentioned data, and then a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) using the imputed dataset. For the GLM, the Gamma family method was chosen as the log of scaled SCI values demonstrates a slight positive skew, therefore it was determined that a Gamma family regression would be worthwhile in highlighting potential relationships in the data, following examination and comparison with the other models.

# Regression and Linear Modelling

# Preparing data for modelling

# Removing duplicate pairs from SCI data

fb_cnt_sci <- fb_cnt_sci[fb_cnt_sci$user_loc < fb_cnt_sci$fr_loc, ]


# Distance dataframe has names as ISO2, all other variables as full country name
# adding ISO2 to all for simplicity - fb data is ISO2

# Adding to GDP data

gdp_pc_sim$C1 <- countrycode(gdp_pc_sim$Country1, "country.name", "iso2c")
gdp_pc_sim$C2 <- countrycode(gdp_pc_sim$Country2, "country.name", "iso2c")

gdp_pc_sim <- gdp_pc_sim %>%
  select("C1", "C2", "Similarity")

# Adding to Language data


language_cle$C1 <- countrycode(language_cle$country_o, "country.name", "iso2c")
language_cle$C2 <- countrycode(language_cle$country_d, "country.name", "iso2c")

language_cle <- language_cle %>%
  select("C1", "C2", "cle")

# Adding to religion data

religion_sim$C1 <- countrycode(religion_sim$Country1, "country.name", "iso2c")
religion_sim$C2 <- countrycode(religion_sim$Country2, "country.name", "iso2c")

religion_sim <- religion_sim %>%
  select("C1", "C2", "Similarity")

# Renaming column names in distance & fb sci dataframes for simplicity of merging

colnames(dist) <- c("C1", "C2", "distance")
colnames(fb_cnt_sci) <- c("C1", "C2", "scaled_sci")
colnames(religion_sim) <- c("C1", "C2", "religious_similarity")
colnames(language_cle) <- c("C1", "C2", "cle")
colnames(gdp_pc_sim) <- c("C1", "C2", "GDP_pc_Similarity")
# Merging into one aggregated dataset


merged_df <- fb_cnt_sci %>%
  left_join(religion_sim, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  left_join(language_cle, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  left_join(dist, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  left_join(gdp_pc_sim, by = c("C1", "C2"))


# Removing country name columns for imputing data

merged_df <- merged_df %>%
  select("scaled_sci", "religious_similarity", "cle", "GDP_pc_Similarity", "distance")

#merged_df <- as.numeric(merged_df)
# Imputing values for Na data for use in a regression model, k estimated at 5 to balance simplicity and model performance
set.seed(42) #setting seed for reproducability


merged_df_imputed <- VIM::kNN(merged_df, k = 5, trace = FALSE)  # k is the number of neighbors

# Creating data set with no NA values through inner_join() function

merged_df_inner <- religion_sim %>%
  inner_join(language_cle, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  inner_join(dist, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  inner_join(gdp_pc_sim, by = c("C1", "C2")) %>%
  inner_join(fb_cnt_sci, by = c("C1", "C2"))

# Inner join drops 6716 rows, in comparison to 'left joined' data

# Log SCI data in imputed and No NA dataset

merged_df_imputed$scaled_sci_log <- log(merged_df_imputed$scaled_sci + 1)  # Adding 1 to avoid log(0)

merged_df_inner$scaled_sci_log <- log(merged_df_inner$scaled_sci + 1)

# Creating regression models
# No NA linear regresssion model
sci_lm_nona <- lm(scaled_sci_log ~ religious_similarity + cle + distance + GDP_pc_Similarity, data = merged_df_inner)

# Imputed data linear regression model
sci_lm_imputed <- lm(scaled_sci_log ~ religious_similarity + cle + distance + GDP_pc_Similarity, data = merged_df_imputed)

# Generalised Linear Model with Gamma distribution and log link for SCI data

sci_glm_imputed_gamma <- glm(scaled_sci_log ~ religious_similarity + cle + distance + GDP_pc_Similarity,
                             data = merged_df_imputed,
                             family = Gamma(link = "log"))

Table 1: Network metrics for a subset of 20 countries in the network

The table highlights network analysis metrics. The first of these, weighted degree, highlights that population and the relative size of nations does not inherently impact SCI. The world’s most populous nation, India, is the country with the lowest weighted degree while South Africa and Argentina have the highest with 4,810,974 and 8,909,020 respectively. This suggests that these nations have significant and meaningfull connections with many nations. Betweeness centrality, a measure of how often a country acts as a bridge between other nations, is 0 for most values - Although a handful of nations such as Japan, India and Mexico have values of 29, 31 and 12 respectively. In the context of SCI data, betweenness centrality may seem irrelevant as all nations have connections with eachother: however it is useful when considering connections with null or negligible values. In this context, nations with high betweenness represent mutual hubs of connectivity between distant communities - that is, groups of nations that are highly connected to a mutual point but not another. While there is some variation in Closeness and Eigenvector centrality, values remain very low and statistical inferences therefore are unproductive.

These statistics provide a general overview country position and importance within the network, although to understand the relationship of countries to each other Louvian community detection is used. The communities identified by the algorithim are demonstrated in Figure 2 below

# plotting community membership using louvain detection algorithm

# Create a custom color palette for communities
community_colors <- hcl.colors(length(unique(membership(community_louvain))), palette = "Dark3")


# Create a list of countries by community
communities_list <- split(V(g)$name, membership(community_louvain))

# Create a formatted legend description that includes countries
legend_descriptions <- sapply(1:length(communities_list), function(i) {
  paste("Community ", i, ": ", paste(communities_list[[i]], collapse = ", "), sep = "")
})


# Plot the network with improvements
plot(community_louvain, g, 
     vertex.size=10,                   # points size
     vertex.label.cex=0.6,              # label size       
     vertex.label.dist=2,               # Adjust label distance from points
     vertex.label.color=rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.5), # Slightly opaque label color (black with 50% opacity)
     edge.width=E(g)$weight / 10,       # Scale edge width based on weight
     edge.color=rgb(0.6, 0.6, 0.6),    # Lighter edge color for better visibility
     main="Community Detection (Louvain Method)",
     col=community_colors[membership(community_louvain)], # Color communities differently
     frame = FALSE,                     # Remove the default frame around the plot
     layout=layout_with_fr)             # Force-directed layout

Figure 2: Abstract graph of community membership for countries in the SCI dataset, determined by Louvain community detection. Colour denotes community membership and countries are labelled by ISO2 code

# Modularity score
modularity_score <- modularity(community_louvain) #0.9297101

# Print modularity score
cat("The modularity score was determined as:", modularity_score, "\n")
## The modularity score was determined as: 0.9299283

Figure 2 demonstrates the community ownership of nations. The algorithim has identified 43 communities which are denoted by colour and labelled by a two letter country code. Interestingly, some communities are limited to one or a few nations, these are typically small and geo-politically isolated nations such as Bhutan and the Bahamas. Large communities appear to be dominated by geographic and cultural proximity. Community 6, for example, comprises the majority of Latin America. A modularity assessment of the Louvian communities found a score of 0.9297 (to 4 decimal places), which suggests a high level of modularity and succesful community detection.

The community data plotted above is represented for all nations in the map below:

# Using world shapefile downloaded previously, from rnaturalearthpackage

# Create a data frame for community memberships
community_membership <- membership(community_louvain)

# Create a data frame of country names and their corresponding community
community_df <- data.frame(Country = names(community_membership), 
                           Community = community_membership)

# Merging with world map shapefile data
world_with_community <- world %>%
  left_join(community_df, by = c("iso_a2" = "Country"))

# Plotting community groups with ggplot2

ggplot(data = world_with_community) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = factor(Community)), color = "white", size = 0.2) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = community_colors, name = "Community") +  # Use community colors
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right") +  # Position legend at the bottom
  labs(title = "Louvain Community Detection on World Map",
       subtitle = "Countries colored by their Louvain community group") +
  theme(legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
        legend.key.size = unit(0.1, "cm"),
        plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12))

Figure 3: World map of countries by community membership

Figure 3 demonstrates the Louvain communities, projected onto cartographic space. The figure highlights the impacts of geographic and cultural proximity, as most communities share a geographic border and exist within the same general locality, exhibiting similar features. Some communities do not follow this trend, such as community number 43, which includes both India and Morocco; objectively geographically and culturally dissimilar nations but closely connected on Facebook. There are examples of clusters containing geographically distant nations with similar religious profiles: such as community number 33, containing buddhist majority Thailand and Mongolia. These open and differing explanations for community membership highlight the need for further analysis.

Linear regression

The specific impacts of the predictor variables were assessed through regression modelling. Linear regression modelling was performed on the assumption that the distribution of SCI is normal. The results of two linear regression models are seen collated below: the first of which was created using only complete data and the second includes imputed values where NA values were present.

          style = "all",
          align = FALSE)

Table 2: Regression Outputs for Two Linear models evaluating the log of scaled SCI against predictor values

Both regression models demonstrate statistical significance at a high (p < 0.01) for all predictor variables and values are relatively similar for all apart from religious similarity - possibly arrising from the large amount of missing data points in the original dataset. Due to this, religious similarity is only significant at p < 0.1 in the imputed dataset. Language similarity has the largest coefficient and is therefore assumed to be the most impactful predictor variable, whilst geographic distance is estimated to have no impact on SCI values. Both models have an acceptable R squared value (0.309 and 0.340 respectively), suggesting that the inclusion of the predictor variables is useful in explaining variance of SCI. To further investigate SCI predictor variables, a GLM was created using the same variables as detailed above. The results of this GLM may be seen in table 3 below.

The table shows that the GLM agrees with the linear regression models in attributing significance to all predictor variables. Whilst created on the same data as the second model above, this GLM finds religious similarity to be significant at p < 0.01. Every coefficient in the GLM is lower than in the linear regression models, whilst distance remains to have no impact. However, the GLM reports a negative log likelihood and high AIC (-29,925.570 and 59,861.140 respectively) suggesting that it does not fit the data as well as the linear regression models.

Discussion

Network Analysis

Table 1 and Table A1 highlight the network analysis metrics produced for this report. The first metric, the weighted degree of each node, suggests that there is a varying level of connectedness for each country. That is, that connectivity is not uniform and nations such as the United States and Argentina are more internationally connected (See Table 1). This should not be assumed to be representative of total social media connectivity as the data set only includes country pairs. However, these higher values may also represent a larger and more active facebook userbase, or higher levels of international interaction.

It is with this in mind that the betweenness centrality measures should be considered. Given that the SCI data is for all possible country-country pairs, betweenness centrality should be null for all (see Barrat et al., 2004). However, upon consideration of the varying levels of connectedness for each nation, and negligible or non-existent SCI values, countries with counts of betweenness centrality may be assumed as common ground between nations that do not connect. To highlight this, many of the nations with high betweenness possess large populations and economies whilst being located in Asia or less economically developed nations, such as India and Mexico. This may suggest that these nations act as a bridge between their primary community of connectivity, and other nations which do not interact with the wider global network. Given that the majority of Betweenness values are zero, it is assumed only a few countries act as such bridges. If this is so, then it would imply that the network is highly fragmented with a handful of countries dominating interaction between self contained clusters.

The values for Closeness and Eigenvector centrality (See Table 1 and A1) are extremely small and demonstrate little variation. Given that the SCI dataset is nearly completely symmetrical and possesses most possible country pairs, this is to be expected and confirms the known structure of the data, however this does not imply that all countries are equally connected, as is disproved by weighted degree.

This initial network analysis confirms that connectivity is not equal between nations and that religion and language may serve to explain a proportion of this variance.

Community Detection

Similar to the findings above, community detection analysis highlights the stratification of country connectedness. This is shown in Figure 2 and 3. In these, the importance of geographic proximity and linguistic similarity are apparent. This is best demonstrated by clusters 6 which comprises the majority of Spanish speaking Latin America.

The figures also highlight isolated communities, such as those comprising of only one or two nations, it is possible that these nations are isolated due to linguistic and cultural values, or for broader geopolitical reasons. Further analysis is required to determine the driving force of these communities.

Regression Modelling

The regression modelling, shown in tables 2 and 3, confirms the importance of the predictor variables included with the model and assumed from community detection. Given the larger variance and smaller coefficient values of the GLM, key findings will be taken from the linear regression model and it is assumed that a Gamma family GLM is not more useful in predicting the log of SCI due to the fairly normal distribution following a log transformation, and that the linear regression models are adequately robust to derive conclusions from.

In these models, language similarity shows a strong and highly significant positive relationship with SCI ( p <0.01), and has the largest coefficient of all variables. This confounds its importance to SCI as suggested by Bailey et al., 2020c. Religious similarity is also found to be statistically significant, although only to a p < 0.10 significance level in the data set that excludes NA values. This may suggest that the effect of religious similarity is more subtle than language and requires a larger data set to highlight this nuance, although it is logical that religious similarity between countries will have a positive impact of connectedness .(See Schwarz and Lynch, 2016). in the models, both of these predictor variables demonstrate a usefulness in predicting SCI and therefore confirms that Religion and Language are important drivers of international connectedness.

Of the two control variables included in the models, GDP per capita similarity was found to be the most impactful, suggesting that nations of similar socio-economic characteristics are more likely to be connected. This is confirmed by previous studies such as Bailey et al., 2018. GDP per capita similarity was found to be statistically significant to a high level of confidence (p < 0.01) in all models. Previous studies have shown geographic distance to be an strong predictor of connectedness (Bailey et al., 2018), however it was found to have a coefficient of zero in all models. Further, the community detection found that most clusters share a border and are not typically geographically dispersed (See figure X). While it is possible that due to the digital, non-geographic nature of facebook friendships that geographic distance is meaningless, this is unlikely due to previous studies that have confirmed its importance. This lack of impact is more likely a result of a methodological flaw in this report or due to colinearity with other variables included in the regression, as opposed to geographic distance not being a useful predictor of SCI.

The findings from the models suggest therefore, that religious, linguistic and socio-economic activity are strong predictors of social connectedness at the country level. From this, with regard to the goal of this study, we assume that language and religion can be used, alongside other variables, to explain the connectedness of countries and play an important role in determining SCI.

Further research

While the findings of this study are useful in demonstrating the importance of religion and language as predictors of SCI, there are limitations present in the study design. Most pertinently, none of the regression models fitted were able to find an effect from geographic distance, despite previous research proving this to be true (Bailey et al., 2018). This is assumed to be a methodological flaw and future research should examine the failings of geographic distance in this study.

More generally, research may build upon this study by increasing the granularity and scope of SCI connections. At the most detailed scale, the SCI data set is available for US - County to County or global adminsitrative subdivision connectedness. This may be further refined by investigating one or a few case studies of specific nations and regions to increase the understanding of drivers behind social connectedness.

Lastly, further research may include a wider range of predictor variables. to explore determinants of SCI. For example Bailey et al., 2018, included mutliple political and demography variables, all of which were found statistically significant at p < 0.01. Additionally, further research into the impacts of language and religion may wish to use unaggregated data, and consider specific religious groups or languages.

Conclusion

This study has investigated the efficacy and validity of religion and language as controls on the connectedness of nations. The primary data source used to estimate the connectedness of nations was the SCI provided by Meta. This data source was firstly investigated from a network analysis perspective, highlighting the symmetrical structure of the dataset, the large variation in individual country connectedness, and the stratification of country communities on a global scale. To explore this last point in greater detail, community analysis was then undertaken to identify sub-sections of the network that are highly connected within their own ‘social sphere’, but with less connections elsewhere. To explain possible controls on these country communities, regression modelling was performed using a combination of cultural (Language and Religion similarity) and control variables (Geographic distance and GDP per capita similarity). Regression analysis highlighted the importance of linguistic similarity as a key determinant of country connectedness, and strongly suggested the importance of religious similarity. However, given possible methodological flaws in the design of this study, as described in the further research section, more work is needed to truly validate the importance of these. Further research investigating the importance of religion and language in influencing the connectedness between nations may wish to refine the methods of this study, potentially addressing the limitations highlighted above, to further investigate the role of language and religion in shaping global connectedness. Additionally, the exploration of other cultural and political factors may improve understanding of the driving forces behind international connections in the digital sphere.
